title: Zigzag Conversion
description: Brute force to optimized: full grid simulation versus direct row buffers versus closed form index arithmetic.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s and a number of rows numRows, write the characters of s in a zigzag pattern across numRows rows, moving straight down one row at a time and then diagonally back up once the bottom row is reached. Read the result row by row, left to right, and return it as a single string.

blocks.text: Given a string s and a number of rows numRows, write the characters of s in a zigzag pattern across numRows rows, moving straight down one row at a time and then diagonally back up once the bottom row is reached. Read the result row by row, left to right, and return it as a single string.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Ball Bouncing Between Two Walls
blocks.text: Picture dropping the characters of the string onto a ball that bounces between the top row and the bottom row as it travels rightward: it falls straight down to the bottom, then bounces back up to the top, over and over. The final answer is simply what has landed in each row, read top row first.

blocks.text: With only one row available, every character already sits in that single row in its original order, so the zigzag pattern has no effect at all and the output equals the input unchanged.
Before writing any code, it is worth asking what a grid actually contributes here, and whether the bounce itself has a structure that could be described directly rather than walked step by step.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A literal two dimensional grid mirroring the visual zigzag shape is mostly empty, since in every column except the first of each cycle, only a single row actually holds a real character.

Observation 2: The grid's only real job is to group characters by which row they belong to, and that grouping can be tracked directly with one growable buffer per row, filled in a single left to right pass, without ever allocating the wasted empty space between rows.

Observation 3: Testing a small example confirms that a simple current-row pointer, bouncing direction only at the very top row and the very bottom row, reproduces the exact same row placement the full grid would have produced.

Observation 4: Since the bounce is perfectly periodic, repeating with a fixed cycle length of two times numRows minus two, exactly which original indices belong to each row can be computed directly with arithmetic, without simulating the bounce character by character at all.
That last observation, a periodic process can be described by a formula instead of walked step by step, is what turns a simulation problem into a direct index calculation.

Allocate an actual two dimensional grid large enough to hold every character at its real zigzag coordinate, walk the string once while computing each character's (row, column) position and placing it in the grid, then read the grid back row by row, skipping the many empty cells that a zigzag pattern always leaves behind.

items: Compute how many columns the grid needs so every cycle of the zigzag fits.
Allocate a numRows by numCols grid, initially empty.
Walk through the string once, tracking the current row and column, moving down until the bottom row and then diagonally up until the top row.
Place each character at its computed grid position.
Read the grid row by row, left to right, appending every non empty cell to the answer.

blocks.caption: Brute force: place every character in a full grid, then scan it to collect the answer

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: numCols is sized generously enough to fit every full down-then-up cycle the string could need, so no character is ever placed outside the allocated grid.
A single boolean direction flag flips exactly at the top row and the bottom row, mirroring the physical bounce described in the analogy directly in code.
The grid is read back in a separate, second pass, row by row, since the fill order and the required read order are different from each other.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every character is placed at the exact grid coordinate the zigzag pattern actually assigns it, and reading the grid back row by row reproduces the required order.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), where n is the length of the string, for the fill pass and the read pass.
Space: O(numRows times numCols), the full grid, which is noticeably larger than the n characters it actually needs to hold since most cells stay empty.
Limitation: allocating a full two dimensional grid wastes memory on cells that are never filled, and the algorithm needs two separate passes, one to fill the grid and another to read it back.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the full grid works but is wasteful: it allocates space for every column position in every row, even though a zigzag pattern only ever places one real character in most of those columns.

What the grid is actually needed for: nothing more than grouping characters by which row they land in, in the order they are encountered.

Can that grouping happen without the wasted grid cells: yes, one growable string buffer per row accomplishes exactly the same grouping, using only as much memory as there are characters.

Can the fill and read steps be merged into one pass: yes, appending each character straight into its own row buffer as it is read means the buffers are already in their final, readable order the moment the pass finishes.

The core idea: keep one buffer per row, bounce a current-row pointer between the top and bottom rows, and append each character directly into its own row's buffer as it is encountered.

The grid's only real job is to group characters by which row they belong to. That grouping can be tracked directly with one growable string buffer per row, updated in a single pass, without ever allocating the unused space between rows. As each character is read from the input, it is appended straight to its own row's buffer, and a simple current row pointer bounces between the top and bottom row exactly the way the ball analogy describes. Once the pass finishes, concatenating the row buffers in order produces the final answer directly, with no separate read step needed.

Keep numRows separate string buffers. Walk through the input once, appending the current character to the current row's buffer, and flip a direction flag whenever the current row hits the top or the bottom, moving the row pointer up or down accordingly. Join all row buffers together at the end.

blocks.caption: Optimized: one pass, appending straight into the current row's own buffer

blocks.text: This works because every character is still assigned to exactly the row the physical bounce would place it in, the direction flag only ever changes at the top row or the bottom row, matching the zigzag definition exactly, and appending straight into each row's own buffer preserves the left to right order within that row automatically, since characters are read from the input in that same left to right order.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass over the string with constant work per character.
Space: O(n), only the row buffers, which together hold exactly the n input characters and nothing more.

The row buffer approach still checks a direction flag on every single character, bouncing it between two branches each time. Since the zigzag pattern is perfectly periodic, with a fixed cycle length equal to two times numRows minus two, exactly which original indices belong to each row can be computed directly with arithmetic, without simulating the bounce character by character at all.
Dry run for row = 1, numRows = 3, s = "PAYPALISHIRING"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Start index (row + k times cycle)","Vertical character","Diagonal offset (start + cycle, minus two times row)","Diagonal character"],"rows":[["1","A","3","P"],["5","L","7","S"],["9","I","11","I"],["13","G","15 (out of range)","none"]]}

items: For each row, every "vertical" character it collects sits at index row, row plus cycle, row plus 2 times cycle, and so on, since the down pass of every cycle visits each row exactly once at a fixed offset.

Only interior rows, strictly between the top and bottom, also collect a "diagonal" character partway through each cycle, since the top and bottom rows are only ever touched by the vertical part of the bounce.

The diagonal offset formula, start plus cycle minus two times row, is derived directly from the fixed cycle length and how far a given interior row sits from the top, and is skipped entirely whenever it would fall past the end of the string.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), every index is visited exactly once across all rows, now with a direct formula instead of a per-character branch.
Space: O(n), for the resulting string.

blocks.text: This is a simulation problem where the real insight is recognizing the fixed, periodic structure of the zigzag pattern: once the cycle length is known, every character's destination row can be described directly instead of walked step by step.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the wasted grid space", think: track only per-row buffers, since that is all the grid was ever really used for.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid simulating the bounce", think: the pattern is periodic, derive which indices belong to each row directly from the fixed cycle length.
If the interviewer says "what happens with numRows equal to 1", think: there is no zigzag at all, return the input unchanged.

items: Why does recognizing a process as periodic let you replace simulation with a direct formula?
How would you adapt this approach if the zigzag needed to bounce between three or more boundary levels instead of just a top and a bottom?
Can you compute, without building the full answer, which row and position a specific original character ends up at?
How would this problem change if characters needed to be read back column by column instead of row by row?
How would you extend the direct index formula to work for numRows equal to 1 without a special case at the very start?
Any simulation problem where the underlying process turns out to be periodic, letting a fixed cycle length replace a step by step walk with direct arithmetic.
Spiral Matrix and similar boundary-bouncing traversal problems, which share this same track-a-direction-and-flip-at-a-boundary structure.
String rearrangement problems in general, where the real question is often just how to group characters by a destination, not how to move them one at a time.
Excel Sheet Column Number and Reverse Integer, which reuse the general idea of finding a closed-form arithmetic relationship instead of simulating a process character by character.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n) time, O(numRows times numCols) space, with wasted grid cells. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space, row buffers only. Further optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space, the same buffers computed via direct index arithmetic instead of a per-character direction check.

items: Pattern: simulation of a perfectly periodic bouncing process, which can be tracked with per-row buffers in one pass, or reduced further to a direct closed form index formula since the bounce repeats with a fixed cycle length.

Core Idea: a grid is only ever needed here to group characters by row, so per-row buffers filled in one pass replace it directly, and since the bounce is periodic with cycle length two times numRows minus two, every row's membership can instead be computed with a direct formula.
Time: O(n) for all three versions.
Space: O(numRows times numCols), mostly wasted, for the brute force; O(n) for both the row-buffer and direct-index versions.
Most Important Observation: a process that bounces or repeats with a fixed period can usually be described by a direct formula instead of simulated step by step.
Interview Difficulty: easy to picture with the bouncing ball analogy; deriving the direct index formula from the cycle length is what shows real understanding of the pattern's structure.
One line memory trick: bounce between row 0 and row numRows minus 1, or skip the bounce entirely using the fixed cycle length, two times numRows minus two.
